questions.knowledge_point: Negating a Sentence Containing a Conjunction
questions.problem:
$\,$ $P$ is not a rhombus and $Q$ is not a rectangle.

What is the negation of the compound statement above?
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,¬(P\text{ is not a rhombus}\text{ and }Q\text{ is not a rectangle}) & ≡¬((P\text{ is not a rhombus})∧(Q\text{ is not a rectangle})) \\  & ≡¬(P\text{ is not a rhombus})∨¬(Q\text{ is not a rectangle}) \\  & ≡(P\text{ is a rhombus})∨(Q\text{ is a rectangle}) \\  & ≡P\text{ is a rhombus}\text{ or }Q\text{ is a rectangle}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Statement Using De Morgan's Laws
questions.problem: Rewrite the statement $¬((¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧¬Q))$ using De Morgan's laws.
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's laws state that

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∧Q)≡¬P∨¬Q, \\ ¬(P∨Q)≡¬P∧¬Q.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify the given statement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬((¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧¬Q)) & ≡¬(¬P∧¬Q)∧¬(P∧¬Q) \\  & ≡(¬(¬P)∨¬(¬Q))∧(¬P∨¬(¬Q)) \\  & ≡(P∨Q)∧(¬P∨Q)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Negating a Sentence Containing a Conjunction
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the negation of the following compound statement? 

$\qquad$ $6$ is composite and $5\!\not{|} \, 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law posits that the negation of a conjunction of two statements is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows.

$$
\neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(6\text{ is composite}\text{ and }5\,\text{⧸}|\,3) & ≡¬((6\text{ is composite})∧(5\,\text{⧸}|\,3)) \\  & ≡¬(6\text{ is composite})∨¬(5\,\text{⧸}|\,3) \\  & ≡(6\text{ is not composite})∨(5\,|\,3) \\  & ≡6\text{ is not composite}\text{ or }5\,|\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Negating a Sentence Containing a Disjunction
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the negation of the following compound statement?

$\qquad$ $3$ is not prime or $\pi$ is not rational.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that the negation of a disjunction of two statements is equivalent to the conjunction of the negations of the individual statements. It can be stated symbolically as follows:

$$
\neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of our statement is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(3\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }\pi \text{ is not rational}) & ≡¬((3\text{ is not prime})∨(\pi \text{ is not rational})) \\  & ≡¬(3\text{ is not prime})∧¬(\pi \text{ is not rational}) \\  & ≡(3\text{ is prime})∧(\pi \text{ is rational}) \\  & ≡3\text{ is prime}\text{ and }\pi \text{ is rational}.\end{aligned}
$$
